title: Infection Control in Neonatal Units
path: High-Risk Neonatal Procedures and Emergency Care

headings.title: Vulnerability of the Neonate to Hospital-Acquired Infections
headings.content: Newborn babies, especially those born preterm or low birth weight, face a very high risk of contracting infections while in the hospital. Their immune systems are immature, meaning their bodies struggle to fight off invading bacteria and viruses. Furthermore, their skin is thin and fragile, breaking down easily under medical tape or sensors, which creates an open door for germs to enter the bloodstream. Routine lifesaving interventions like endotracheal tubes, intravenous lines, and urinary catheters bypass the body's natural physical barriers. Once a pathogen enters through these routes, it can spread rapidly throughout a tiny body because localized inflammatory responses are weak in neonates.

headings.title: Hand Hygiene Protocols for Midwives and Staff
headings.content:
Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention to stop cross-contamination in a neonatal unit. Midwives and healthcare workers must clean their hands before and after touching any baby, touching equipment, or performing invasive procedures. 

- **Alcohol-Based Rub**: Use when hands are visibly clean, rubbing all surfaces for at least twenty seconds.
- **Soap and Water**: Mandatory when hands are visibly soiled with body fluids or after caring for a baby with a known enteric infection like rotavirus.
- **Surgical Scrub**: Required before entering sterile procedures, using antiseptic soap for a longer duration.

A common mistake in busy wards is rushing the drying process or wearing rings and long artificial nails that harbor colonies of bacteria beneath them.

headings.title: Standard and Isolation Precautions in the Nursery
headings.content:
Standard precautions apply to the care of all newborns, treating all blood, body fluids, secretions, and non-intact skin as potential carriers of infection. When a specific pathogen is identified or suspected, transmission-based precautions are added. 

- **Contact Precautions**: Used for organisms spread by direct touch, such as multi-resistant organisms, requiring gowns and gloves.
- **Droplet Precautions**: Used for pathogens transmitted through large respiratory particles, requiring masks when working close to the infant.
- **Airborne Precautions**: Used for infections spread through fine aerosol particles, requiring special negative pressure rooms where available.

Cohort nursing—grouping babies with the exact same infection together with dedicated staff—helps prevent the spread of outbreaks in crowded nurseries.

headings.title: Environmental Cleaning and Equipment Sterilization
headings.content: The neonatal environment harbors many surfaces that can easily transfer pathogens if neglected. Incubators, radiant warmers, phototherapy lights, and monitoring leads require regular, systematic disinfection using hospital-approved cleaning agents. Non-critical items like cots need low-level disinfection, while semi-critical items like respiratory tubing require high-level disinfection. Critical items that enter sterile tissues, such as surgical instruments and central venous catheters, must undergo complete sterilization. Midwives must verify that contact times recommended by the manufacturer are strictly followed, because wiping a surface down and drying it instantly does not allow the disinfectant enough time to kill resistant spores.

headings.title: Rational Antibiotic Stewardship and Surveillance
headings.content: Overusing broad-spectrum antibiotics in the neonatal unit breeds resistant strains of bacteria that become nearly impossible to treat. Antibiotic stewardship involves prescribing antimicrobials only when clinically justified, using culture results to narrow treatment choices, and stopping therapy promptly if cultures return negative. Surveillance systems track infection rates across the ward to spot unusual clusters or rising trends early. Midwives play a vital role in reporting subtle clinical changes in neonates, such as temperature instability, poor feeding, or lethargy, which often serve as the earliest warning signs of sepsis before lab results confirm it.
